I'm interested in this game for its historic importance.

So far the game received $117 million in funding. To put this number in perspective, here's a list of games with the biggest budgets. Some of the more notable titles (numbers are inflation adjusted and include marketing costs):

GTA V: 269M
Star Wars TOR: 210M
GTA IV: 110M
Skyrim: 89M
Witcher 3: 81M
HL2: 50M
World of Warcraft: 50M

These games were developed with experienced, in-house teams based on existing IP. They had experienced artists, game developers as well as experienced project managers that most of whom worked together in the past. Star Citizen bucks the trend. Chris Roberts -- the Cloud Imperium Games (CIG) founder -- has little to no experience managing projects of this size. The team hired to develop the game is all new. Some work is outsourced to other companies.

After four or five years in development the game still describes itself as being pre-alpha. Despite statements by Chris Roberts that the final product would be released in less time at a fraction of what has been invested so far, the promises did not materialize. It is my understanding that the bulk of the money has already been spent on development, with about $8 million left in reserve. There seems to be little or no accountability for how the money is spent. Nor is there an estimate for when the game will be released with even the most optimistic players giving a time estimate of "a few years". The sentiment is that it's better to take the time to do things right rather than to release an unfinished game. The company employs somewhere between 150 to 300 employees (I'm not sure of the exact number) and needs ongoing fundraising to pay its bills.

Selling ships is how the bulk of fundraising is done. To get access to the game you must buy a package which consists of one or more ships. The prices range from $45 for a small starter ship to $15000 a large number of ships. Some of the more expensive ships exist only as concept art and have not yet been created. There are also some limited, time, limited availability ships for sale for upwards of $2500. What advantages or disadvantages various ships will have in the final game is anyone's guess.

They are also taking $45 pledges for a single player shooter game called Squadron 42 set in the Star Citizen universe to be released in 2017. Reception to the news among backers has been positive despite the development effort now being split between two games while the main game is nowhere near being finished.

Much of /r/starcitizen is in denial about problems with the game:

This backer tries to approximate the number of sales for Star Citizen when it's released. Screenshot
To say that he's over optimistic would be a vast understatement. Note his Flair of Lt. Commander. That's a $2500 backer.

This backer explains their relationship with CIG. It sounds like he's describing an abusive relationship. Screenshot
"He only beats me for a few months at a time. Then he rewards me with sex and he's the most awesome person in the world for about two weeks."

A common meme is that CIG is sitting on a stockpile of assets and new feature. Screenshot
Excuses such as "You can't eat steak every day" abound.

Thoughts and tidbits:

  • The pace of game development with regards to new features is slow. I'm not much of a developer, but the project's codebase smells. It's as if the initial design did not scale well or isn't flexible enough. Changes made to code have unpredictable effects. Players are seeing many bizarre bugs. It makes sense that CIG is focusing more on releasing SQ42 to get something out there to appease the players.
  • They have a pretty good pipeline for producing ships. Ships are essentially art assets which don't require much involvement from the devs to create. The process scales linearly with the resources thrown at it. Need to raise more money? Hire more artists and make even more ships.
  • The game is reminiscent of Scientology where the backers are buying ships instead of Operating Thetan levels. Backers are in denial about the state of the game. There is no shortage of excuses for any aspect of the game or any broken promise. Some are talking about having "faith" in the game.
  • Probably the only game in pre-alpha to have a yearly convention. Certainly the only pre-alpha game to have over 1000 attendees.
  • Chris Robert's wife, Sandi Gardiner, is the vice president of the company.
  • Backers can have their accounts banned for actions outside of Star Citizen forums or game, such as criticism of the game.
  • Game runs at about 20-30fps even on the best hardware.
  • Game developers unaffiliated with Star Citizen claim that what Star Citizen promised -- a seamless world with thousands of players -- is impossible to do using CryEngine.

I don't think the game as it was originally promised will ever be released. Squadron 42 might get released in late 2017/early 2018. Meanwhile the company is burning through $10-20 million per year so we'll continue to see constant fundraising drives. When selling ships is milked dry they'll invent some new imaginary asset to sell. Space stations? Planets? Star systems? Who knows. Squadron 42 will be a disappointment. CIG will find it difficult to raise more funds as even the most skeptical backers become disillusioned. CIG will plead that "we just need a little bit more money to finish the game" and "this is the home stretch" and "if we don't get more money then the whole thing will have been for naught." 2020 or 2021 Star Citizen will be released as an instanced MMO instead of the seamless world they promised. Lawsuits will be filed.

In the beginning of this post I mentioned that I'm interested in the game for its historic importance. The game will be seen for what it is -- the biggest failure of crowdfunding in history. There will be calls for more regulation of crowdfunding comparing the failure to Enron.
